title: Midterm Project
text:
Introduction
Life expectancy is widely used as a summary measure of population health and overall social development, and understanding the factors associated with life expectancy can help provide insight into global differences in living conditions. In this project, we analyze global data from 2000 to 2020 to explore how life expectancy varies across countries and how it relates to several socioeconomic, demographic, and environmental indicators. The variables used in our analysis include: GDP per capita, health expenditure, population aged 65 and older, secondary school enrollment rates, PM2.5 air pollution levels and fertility rates. In addition, country-level categorical information such as region and income group is also included to examine patterns of certain groups.

title: Midterm Project
text:
Methods and Preliminary Results
The data used in this analysis is from the World Bank World Development Indicators through the World Bank API. For each selected indicator, we fetch observations for all countries between 2000 and 2020 using API requests, and then merged into a single dataset based on country and year. Additional country metadata is merged with the indicator dataset using ISO2 country codes.

variables = {
    "life_expectancy": "SP.DYN.LE00.IN",
    "gdp_per_capita": "NY.GDP.PCAP.CD",
    "health_expenditure": "SH.XPD.CHEX.GD.ZS",
    "pop_65plus": "SP.POP.65UP.TO.ZS",
    "school_enrollment": "SE.SEC.ENRR",
    "pm25_pollution": "EN.ATM.PM25.MC.M3",
    "fertility_rate": "SP.DYN.TFRT.IN"
}

def fetch_indicator(name, code, start_year=2000, end_year=2020):
    url = f"https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/all/indicator/{code}?format=json&date={start_year}:{end_year}&per_page=20000"
    response = requests.get(url)
    if response.status_code != 200:
        print(f"Error fetcing data for {name}")
        return pd.DataFrame()
    data = response.json()
    if len(data) < 2:
        return pd.DataFrame()
    df = pd.DataFrame(data[1])
    df = df[["country", "date", "value"]]
    df.columns = ["Country", "Year", name]
    df["Year"] = df["Year"].astype(int)
    df["Country"] = df["Country"].str["id"]
    return df

dfs = []
for name, code in variables.items():
    df = fetch_indicator(name, code)
    if not df.empty:
        print(f"Fetched data for {name}")
        dfs.append(df)
    time.sleep(0.1)

merged = dfs[0]
for df in dfs[1:]:
    merged = merged.merge(df, how="outer", on=["Country", "Year"])

After merging the datasets, we first remove missing values to ensure consistency. Aggregate entries representing groups of countries or regions are also excluded so that the analysis focuses only on individual countries. After examining the summary statistics, observations with unrealistically low life expectancy values, in this case life expectancy under 40 years, are removed.

The histogram shows that most countries fall within a broad range between approximately 60 and 80 years, though some countries exhibit considerably lower values. A time series of the global average life expectancy shows a generally increasing trend from 2000 to 2020, with a dip at 2020 likely due to Covid. Comparisons across income groups show that high-income countries consistently achieve higher life expectancy, while low-income countries tend to have lower values. Regional comparisons similarly highlight disparities, with Sub-Saharan Africa exhibiting significantly lower average life expectancy than other regions. The scatter plots suggest several potentially meaningful relationships between life expectancy and the selected variables. Countries with higher GDP per capita, a larger share of the population aged 65 and above, and higher secondary school enrollment rates tend to have higher life expectancy, indicating positive correlations between these variables and overall population health. In contrast, PM2.5 air pollution and fertility rate show negative relationships with life expectancy, countries with higher pollution levels or higher fertility rates generally have lower life expectancy. Health expenditure as a percentage of GDP does not appear to show a clear relationship with life expectancy in the scatter plots, suggesting little to no correlation.

The exploratory analysis suggests that our chosen list of indicators are associated with differences in life expectancy across countries, as mentioned in the preliminary results part above. A simple OLS regression model shows several significant relationships between life expectancy and the selected variables. GDP per capita, the share of the population aged 65 and above, and secondary school enrollment are all positively associated with life expectancy. Fertility rate shows a very strong negative correlation. Health expenditure as a percentage of GDP has a small positive association. PM2.5 pollution also has a positive coefficient in the regression, which differs from common sense and the negative pattern observed in the scatter plots. All the coefficients of the predictors have a p-value lower than 0.05, suggesting statistical significance.
For the final project, several ML models will be explored to predict life expectancy based on the selected indicators, including linear regression models, GAMs and random forests. Model performance will be evaluated using CV methods. The results will be presented through interactive visualizations on our deployed website.

title: JSC370 Final Project
text:
Life expectancy is widely used as a summary measure of population health and overall social development, and understanding the factors associated with life expectancy can help provide insight into global differences in living conditions. In this project, we analyze global data from 2000 to 2020 to explore how life expectancy varies across countries and how it relates to several socioeconomic, demographic, and environmental indicators. Understanding these patterns is useful for identifying which factors appear most strongly associated with longer lives.


TThe data used in this analysis is from the World Bank World Development Indicators through the World Bank API, from 2000 to 2020. The World Bank WDI database is a well-known source for global development statistics, providing standardized data that allows for rigorous studies.



Which socioeconomic, demographic, and environmental indicators serve as the most significant determinants of life expectancy, and to what extent do these factors vary in influence across different global regions and income groups?



Building on the midterm analysis, the final project shifts to a predictive modelling task. The central objective is to determine whether these socioeconomic, demographic, and environmental variables can accurately predict life expectancy across countries and years, and which predictors are most influential once modeled jointly.
To ensure numerical stability and model interpretability, the models will use the following factors as tentative predictors: - Economic: GDP per capita. - Health: Health expenditure. - Demographic: Fertility rates and population age 65+. - Education: Secondary school enrollment. - Environmental: PM2.5 pollution. - Contextual: Geographic region and income group.

title: JSC370 Final Project
text:
Data Preprocessing

Feature Engineering
These engineered features were chosen to improve model stability and interpretability while preserving interpretability.

log_gdp_per_capita: We use the natural log of GDP per capita to reduce right-skew and limit the influence of very high-income outliers. This usually makes the relationship with life expectancy smoother and easier to model.
absolute_health_spending: We convert health expenditure from a percentage into an absolute value per capita. This gives a more interpretable healthcare spending measure across countries with very different income levels.
year_norm: We subtract 2000 from the year values to improve numerical stability and interpretation, especially in regression models where raw year values are too large.
income_group_ord: We manually encode income group as an ordinal variable to preserve the rank structure.
region: We use one-hot encoding on region, so no artificial ranking is imposed on regions.



Train/Test Split
We first drop the country column as it can’t be a predictor, then split using a 70/30 ratio with random state of 370 for reproducibility. All models are trained on the train split and evaluated only on the held out test split. The dimensions of the splits are as follows:

title: JSC370 Final Project
text:
Models

Preparations


Model 1: Generalized Additive Model
The generalized additive model estimates life expectancy as a sum of smooth effects from predictors. This allows nonlinear relationships while keeping the contribution of each feature interpretable.


Model 2: Random Forest
Random Forest is an ensemble of decision trees fit on bootstrap samples with random feature selection at splits. We use a parameter grid to tune the hyperparameters, and the best setting is selected by cross validation.


Model 3: XGBoost
XGBoost is a boosted tree model that builds trees sequentially to try to reduce prior residual error. Similar to the random forest model, we use the parameter grid to tune the hyperparameters, and the best setting is also selected by cross validation.

title: JSC370 Final Project
text:
Variable Importance
Checking the importance of the variables are crucial as they help us figure out which variables are actually making an impact on life expectancy. Here we take the top 10 most important features from the two better preforming models: the random forest model and the XGBoost model, and compare them.

Random Forest











XGBoost









Feature importance results from both models are broadly consistent, as shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5b.
In Figure 5a, the top predictors for Random Forest are fertility rate, region being Sub-Saharan Africa, and logged GDP per capita. In Figure 5b, the most influential features for XGBoost are region being Sub-Saharan Africa, fertility rate, and absolute health expenditure.
The XGBoost model seems to put high emphasis on the region dummy variables, while the random forest model not as much. The overlapping variables are fertility rates, logged GDP per capita, absolute health expenditure, year, and region being Sub-Saharan Africa and Middle East and North Africa. Across both models, the overlap in highly ranked variables suggests that these predictors carry robust signal for explaining cross-country variation in life expectancy.
